References

On this page

Spheroids and ellipsoids by the multipole expansion ​

The whole page as one script

Every block of this page, in order, is scripts/99_multipole_spheroids.jl. From a clone of the repository, julia --project=docs -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' once, then julia scripts/99_multipole_spheroids.jl, runs it end to end.

Before this page

The multipole expansion method for spheroids and for ellipsoids, where the scheme is derived, with anisotropic constituents, for spheroids in elasticity, for ellipsoids in elasticity, and Particle assemblies and N-body schemes for the assemblies it acts on.

Kushch et al. (2015) give the conductivity of oblate spheroids on three lattices, with a perfect interface, a low-conducting (Kapitza) one and a highly conducting one. This page computes the same quantities with MultipoleExpansion and sets them beside the published values, read from the files below. It goes on with the stiffness of spheroids bonded by a spring (Kushch, 2018), with ellipsoids bonded by a Kapitza interface (Kushch, 2020), with spheroids in a transversely isotropic matrix (Kushch and Sevostianov, 2014), with the stiffness of lattices of spheroids (Kushch, 2013), and with ellipsoids bonded by springs (Kushch, 2019).

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization
using TensND
using LinearAlgebra
using JSON
using Markdown
using Printf
using Plots
gr()

# Interactive 3D helpers (Plotly through require.js).
include(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "scripts", "common", "docviz.jl"))

default(; left_margin = 5Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm)

paper = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "kushch2015.json"))
quantity(name) = paper["quantities"][name]["value"]
Data read above: data/literature/kushch2015.json 4 quantities, 50 records

Kushch, Volodymyr I., Sevostianov, Igor, Belyaev, A. S. (2015). Effective conductivity of spheroidal particle composite with imperfect interfaces: Complete solutions for periodic and random micro structures. Mechanics of Materials 89, 1-11. doi:10.1016/j.mechmat.2015.05.010

Read in Tables 1 to 8, pp. 6-9 checked against the source

Transcribed from the published article (PDF), read on the page text

Conductivities are divided by that of the matrix. All tables are for oblate spheroids of aspect ratio e = l3/l1 = 1/3, aligned with the axis x3. The low-conducting (Kapitza) interface has the parameter hc_tilde = l1 hc/k0 with the contrast k1/k0 = 1000; the highly conducting interface has hs_tilde = hs/(l1 k0) with k1/k0 = 0.1. The lattices are proportional: periods a1 = a2 and a3 = e a1; SP holds one spheroid per cell, BCP two (shift (a1, a2, a3)/2), FCP four (shifts (a1, 0, a3)/2, (a1, a2, 0)/2, (0, a2, a3)/2).

Notes

  • Table maxwell_lc: Table 1, p. 6. Maxwell estimate (one spheroid), low-conducting interface; columns hc_tilde = 1, 10 and infinity (perfect).
  • Table maxwell_hc: Table 2, p. 6. Maxwell estimate (one spheroid), highly conducting interface; columns hs_tilde = 0, 1 and 10.
  • Table convergence_sp: Table 3, p. 7. SP lattice, c = 0.5, low-conducting interface: convergence with the truncation tmax. The finite-element row printed under it is the quantity fem_sp_c05.
  • Table lattices_perfect: Table 4, p. 8. Perfect interface, contrast 1000. Columns k11_<lattice> and k33_<lattice> for the SP, BCP and FCP lattices and the random (RND) structure, the latter an average over 100 cells of 30 spheroids, printed with fewer digits.

  • Table lattices_lc_10: Table 6, p. 8. Low-conducting interface, hc_tilde = 10, contrast 1000. Columns k11_<lattice> and k33_<lattice> for the SP, BCP and FCP lattices and the random (RND) structure, the latter an average over 100 cells of 30 spheroids, printed with fewer digits.

1. The lattices ​

The spheroids are oblate, of semi-axes   with  , aligned with . The lattices are proportional: the cell has the periods , and holds one spheroid (SP), two (BCP, the second at the center of the cell) or four (FCP, the others at the centers of three faces). The fraction sets . The interface is carried by a one-layer LayeredSpheroid: a KapitzaInterface of resistance for the low-conducting interface, of parameter   , and a SurfaceConductiveInterface of conductance for the highly conducting one, of parameter   .

julia
e = quantity("aspect_ratio")
k₀ = TensISO{3}(1.0)
sites = Dict(
    "sp" => [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)],
    "bcp" => [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)],
    "fcp" => [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), (0.5, 0.0, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.0), (0.0, 0.5, 0.5)],
)
semi_axis(kind, c) = cbrt(3c / (4π * length(sites[kind])))

function lattice(kind, c; k₁, interface = l₁ -> PerfectInterface{Float64}())
    l₁ = semi_axis(kind, c)
    asm = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = PeriodicBox((1.0, 1.0, e)))
    add_matrix!(asm, Dict(:K => k₀))
    for (i, x) in enumerate(sites[kind])
        spheroid = LayeredSpheroid((e * l₁,), (l₁,), (TensISO{3}(k₁),); interfaces = (interface(l₁),))
        add_particle!(asm, Symbol(:p, i), (x[1], x[2], e * x[3]), spheroid, Dict(:K => TensISO{3}(k₁)))
    end
    return asm
end

kapitza(h̃c) = l₁ -> KapitzaInterface(l₁ / h̃c)
surface(h̃s) = l₁ -> SurfaceConductiveInterface(h̃s * l₁)
conductivity(asm, nmax) = (K = canonical_components(homogenize(asm, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax), :K)); (K[1, 1], K[3, 3]))

The body-centered cell at  , with the spheroids of the neighboring cells that overlap it:

julia
function cell_scene(asm; uid)
    traces = String[]
    for name in particle_names(asm), shift in Iterators.product(-1:1, -1:1, -1:1)
        X₀ = particle_center(asm, name) .+ shift .* (1.0, 1.0, e)
        all(-0.6 .≤ X₀ ./ (1.0, 1.0, e) .≤ 0.6) || continue
        a, b = MeanFieldHomogenization.LayeredSpheroids.outer_semiaxes(particle_geometry(asm, name))
        X, Y, Z = ellipsoid_surface(b, b, a; center = X₀, nu = 25, nv = 13)
        push!(traces, surface_trace(X, Y, Z; color = "#4063D8"))
    end
    return plotly_scene(traces; uid, height = 480, title = "oblate spheroids of aspect ratio 1/3 on the BCP lattice, c = 0.4")
end

cell_scene(lattice("bcp", 0.4; k₁ = 1.0); uid = "mem-bcp-spheroids")

2. Convergence on the simple lattice ​

At   the spheroids of the simple lattice nearly touch, by a gap of along their axis. The table gives against the truncation degree, computed and, in parentheses, published, for the conductivity ratio  . Only the odd degrees enter: every spheroid being a center of symmetry of the lattice, the field it receives under a uniform gradient is odd about it.

julia
k₁ = quantity("contrast_lc")
perfect = l₁ -> PerfectInterface{Float64}()
columns = (("perfect", "hc_infinity", perfect), ("``\\tilde h_c = 10``", "hc_10", kapitza(10.0)), ("``\\tilde h_c = 1``", "hc_1", kapitza(1.0)))
function convergence_table(rows)
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``n_{\\\\max}`` | ", join(first.(columns), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "| :-- | ", join(fill(":--", length(columns)), " | "), " |")
    for row in rows
        cells = map(columns) do (_, key, interface)
            k11, k33 = conductivity(lattice("sp", 0.5; k₁, interface), row["tmax"])
            @sprintf("%.3f, %.3f (%.3f, %.3f)", k11, k33, row["k11_$key"], row["k33_$key"])
        end
        println(io, "| ", row["tmax"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end
convergence_table(r for r in paper["tables"]["convergence_sp"] if r["tmax"] ≤ 7)

The published values agree with the computed ones to the last printed digit at every degree: the truncation is the same, and so is the solution. The perfect interface converges slowly, as the article notes; a resistance at the interface smooths the field and the degree 5 suffices.

3. Three lattices, three interfaces ​

Each cell gives computed at nmax = 7 and, in parentheses, published.

julia
function lattices_table(table, k₁, interface; cs = (0.1, 0.2), nmax = 7)
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``c`` | SP | BCP | FCP |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for row in paper["tables"][table]
        row["c"] in cs || continue

            @sprintf("%.3f, %.3f (%.3f, %.3f)", k11, k33, row["k11_$kind"], row["k33_$kind"])
        end
        println(io, "| ", row["c"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")

The arrangement matters: with the perfect interface, the FCP lattice conducts a quarter more than the simple one in the plane of the spheroids at  , and less along their axis. Denser lattices need higher degrees: on the simple lattice at  , reaches its published value 2.016 at nmax = 13 (2.016 computed), against 1.971 at nmax = 7. The random arrangements of the article, averaged over a hundred cells, are not reproduced here.

4. The interface parameter ​

The conductivities of the simple lattice at   against the parameter of the low-conducting interface, beside the Mori–Tanaka estimate built on the same layered spheroid. The latter is the Maxwell estimate of the article, Table 1, which it recovers:

julia
function maxwell_table()
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``\\\\tilde h_c`` | ``(k_{11}, k_{33})/k_0`` at ``c = 0.5`` | published |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    row = only(r for r in paper["tables"]["maxwell_lc"] if r["c"] == 0.5)
    for (label, key, interface) in (("1", "hc_1", kapitza(1.0)), ("10", "hc_10", kapitza(10.0)), ("∞", "hc_infinity", perfect))
        K = canonical_components(homogenize(lattice("sp", 0.5; k₁, interface), MoriTanaka(), :K))
        println(io, @sprintf("| %s | %.3f, %.3f | %.3f, %.3f |", label, K[1, 1], K[3, 3], row["k11_$key"], row["k33_$key"]))
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

The single-particle estimate misses the interactions over the whole range: it overestimates and underestimates , the two curves of crossing only near  , and the gap grows with .

5. Elastic spheroids with a spring interface ​

Kushch (2018) treats one spheroid with a spring interface of equal normal and tangential stiffnesses , of parameter  , and gives the Maxwell estimate of aligned spheroids at the fraction 0.3,  ,  ,  . For aligned spheroids that estimate is Mori–Tanaka, computed here on the elastic layered spheroid. Each cell gives , computed and, in parentheses, published.

julia
elastic = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "kushch2018.json"))
iso(μ, ν) = TensISO{3}(2μ * (1 + ν) / (1 - 2ν), 2μ)
eq(name) = elastic["quantities"][name]["value"]
C₀ = iso(1.0, eq("nu0"))
C₁ = iso(eq("mu_ratio"), eq("nu1"))
function spring_estimate(e, D̃)
    D = D̃ / max(1.0, e)
    spheroid = LayeredSpheroid((e,), (1.0,), (C₁,); interfaces = (SpringInterface(D, D),))
    s = cbrt(eq("fraction"))
    asm = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = MixedBC(Ellipsoid(1 / s, 1 / s, e / s)))
    add_matrix!(asm, Dict(:C => C₀))
    add_particle!(asm, :p, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), spheroid, Dict(:C => C₁))
    M = mandel(homogenize(asm, MoriTanaka(), :C), CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
    return (M[1, 1], M[3, 3], M[4, 4] / 2)
end
function spring_table()
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``\\\\tilde D`` | ``e = 1/3`` | ``e = 3`` |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    rows = elastic["tables"]["maxwell_aligned"]
    for D̃ in (1.0e-6, 1.0, 10.0, 1.0e6)
        cells = map((1 / 3, 3.0)) do e
            row = only(r for r in rows if r["e"] ≈ e && r["D"] == D̃)
            C = spring_estimate(e, D̃)
            @sprintf("%.4f, %.4f, %.4f (%.4f, %.4f, %.4f)", C..., row["C11"], row["C33"], row["C44"])
        end
        println(io, "| ", D̃, " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

Through a soft spring ( ) spheroids a hundred times stiffer than the matrix lower all its moduli (    and   in the matrix alone); through a stiff one they act as perfectly bonded.

6. Ellipsoids with a Kapitza interface ​

Kushch (2020) gives the Maxwell estimate of ellipsoids of semi-axes at the fraction 0.5, conductivity ratio 100, against the conductance of a Kapitza interface and the degree. One InterfacedEllipsoid in a domain of its own shape is that estimate; each cell gives the computed value and, in parentheses, the published one.

julia
ellipsoids = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "kushch2020.json"))
semi = Tuple(ellipsoids["quantities"]["semi_axes"]["value"])
function ellipsoid_estimate(hc, nmax)
    c = ellipsoids["quantities"]["fraction"]["value"]
    asm = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = MixedBC(Ellipsoid((semi ./ cbrt(c))...)))
    add_matrix!(asm, Dict(:K => k₀))
    particle = InterfacedEllipsoid(semi..., KapitzaInterface(1 / hc))
    add_particle!(asm, :p, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), particle, Dict(:K => TensISO{3}(ellipsoids["quantities"]["contrast"]["value"])))
    return canonical_components(homogenize(asm, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax), :K))[1, 1]
end
function ellipsoid_table()
    io = IOBuffer()
    hcs = (("hc_1e-2", 1.0e-2), ("hc_1", 1.0), ("hc_1e2", 1.0e2))
    println(io, "| ``n_{\\\\max}`` | ", join(("``h_c = $(h)``" for (_, h) in hcs), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for row in ellipsoids["tables"]["maxwell_kapitza"]
        row["nmax"] ≤ 5 || continue
        cells = [@sprintf("%.7f (%.7f)", ellipsoid_estimate(h, row["nmax"]), row[key]) for (key, h) in hcs]
        println(io, "| ", row["nmax"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

7. Spheroids in a transversely isotropic matrix ​

Kushch and Sevostianov (2014) consider spheroids of semi-axes and conductivity   in a matrix of conductivities   across and   along , on an orthorhombic lattice of periods proportional to the semi-axes. They tabulate the anisotropy parameter  , which measures how much the particles change the anisotropy of the matrix. The scheme maps the matrix to an isotropic one (see the theory), where the spheroids become spheroids of semi-axis ratio , or spheres when  , of anisotropic conductivity.

julia
anisotropy = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "kushch2014.json"))
function anisotropy_parameter(e, κ, c, nmax)
    semi = (1.0, 1.0, e)
    cell = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = PeriodicBox(cbrt(4π / 3 / c) .* semi))
    add_matrix!(cell, Dict(:K => TensTI{2}(1.0, κ, (0.0, 0.0, 1.0))))
    inclusion = anisotropy["quantities"]["inclusion_conductivity"]["value"]
    add_particle!(cell, :p, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), Ellipsoid(semi...), Dict(:K => TensISO{3}(inclusion)))
    k = diag(canonical_components(homogenize(cell, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax), :K)))
    return (k[3] / κ) / k[1]
end
function anisotropy_table(nmax)
    io = IOBuffer()
    fractions = ("0.15", "0.30", "0.40")
    println(io, "| ``e`` | ``\\\\kappa`` | ", join(("``c = $(c)``" for c in fractions), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for row in anisotropy["tables"]["anisotropy_ti"]
        cells = map(fractions) do c
            computed, published = anisotropy_parameter(row["aspect_ratio"], row["matrix_anisotropy"], parse(Float64, c), nmax), row["c_$c"]
            cell = @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", computed, published)
            abs(computed - published) > 1.0e-3 ? "**$(cell)**" : cell
        end
        println(io, "| ", row["aspect_ratio"], " | ", row["matrix_anisotropy"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

8. Stiffness of lattices of spheroids ​

Kushch (2013), Table 7.6, gives of spheroids of semi-axes on an orthogonal lattice of periods proportional to them, with   , against the shear modulus ratio (zero for cavities) and the volume fraction. The spheres,  , are those of the application Arrays and clusters of spheres by the multipole expansion; the oblate spheroids follow, at the fraction 0.1 for both shapes and 0.3 for  .

julia
book = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "kushch2013.json"))
poisson_iso(μ) = TensISO{3}(2μ * 1.3 / 0.4, 2μ)          # (3κ, 2μ) at ν = 0.3
function lattice_stiffness(ε, μ₁, c, nmax)
    semi = (1.0, 1.0, ε)
    cell = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = PeriodicBox(cbrt(4π / 3 / c) .* semi))
    add_matrix!(cell, Dict(:C => poisson_iso(1.0)))
    add_particle!(cell, :p, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), Ellipsoid(semi...), Dict(:C => poisson_iso(μ₁)))
    M = TensND.mandel(homogenize(cell, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax), :C), TensND.CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
    return M[3, 3]
end
function lattice_table()
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``\\\\varepsilon`` | ``\\\\mu_1/\\\\mu_0`` | ``c = 0.1`` | ``c = 0.3`` |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for row in book["tables"]["stiffness_spheroids"]
        ε, μ₁ = row["aspect_ratio"], row["contrast"]
        ε < 1 || continue
        # a flat cavity converges more slowly in the degree
        low = @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", lattice_stiffness(ε, μ₁, 0.1, ε == 0.2 && μ₁ == 0 ? 8 : 6), row["c_0.1"])
        high = ε == 0.5 ? @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", lattice_stiffness(ε, μ₁, 0.3, 8), row["c_0.3"]) : "–"
        println(io, "| ", ε, " | ", μ₁, " | ", low, " | ", high, " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

9. Ellipsoids bonded by springs ​

Kushch (2019), Table 5, gives the Maxwell estimate of ellipsoids of semi-axes at the volume fraction 0.5, with  ,  ,  , bonded by springs of equal normal and tangential stiffness , from the perfect bond to the cavity. One InterfacedEllipsoid in a domain of its own shape is that estimate; the rows   and   are recovered with the stiffness   (the text of the article states  ).

julia
springs = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "kushch2019a.json"))
spring_q(k) = springs["quantities"][k]["value"]
function ellipsoid_spring_estimate(D)
    semi = Tuple(spring_q("semi_axes"))
    ν_iso(μ, ν) = TensISO{3}(2μ * (1 + ν) / (1 - 2ν), 2μ)
    cell = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = MixedBC(Ellipsoid((semi ./ cbrt(spring_q("fraction")))...)))
    add_matrix!(cell, Dict(:C => ν_iso(1.0, spring_q("nu0"))))
    C₁ = D == 0 ? TensISO{3}(0.0, 0.0) : ν_iso(spring_q("mu_ratio"), spring_q("nu1"))
    particle = D isa Number && D > 0 ? InterfacedEllipsoid(semi..., SpringInterface(D, D)) : Ellipsoid(semi...)
    add_particle!(cell, :p, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), particle, Dict(:C => C₁))
    return TensND.mandel(homogenize(cell, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax = 8), :C), TensND.CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
end
function ellipsoid_spring_table()
    io = IOBuffer()
    entries = (("C1111", 1, 1), ("C3333", 3, 3), ("C2233", 2, 3), ("C1212", 6, 6))
    println(io, "| ``D`` | ", join(("``C_{$(k[2:end])}/\\\\mu_0``" for (k, _, _) in entries), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for row in springs["tables"]["maxwell_spring"]
        D = row["D"] == "Infinity" ? Inf : row["D"]
        M = ellipsoid_spring_estimate(D)
        cells = [@sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", M[i, j] / (i > 3 ? 2 : 1), row[k]) for (k, i, j) in entries]
        println(io, "| ", row["D"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

10. Arrays of penny-shaped cracks ​

Kushch (2013), Tables 6.3, 7.7 and 7.8, gives the conductivity of a solid with insulating cracks, and its moduli and with traction-free cracks,  , the cracks of unit radius and normal lying on the lattice of periods (theory). The moduli follow from the effective compliance as   and  .

julia
function crack_cell(a, a₃, property)
    cell = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = PeriodicBox((a, a, a₃)))
    add_matrix!(cell, property)
    add_particle!(cell, :c, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), EllipticCrack(1.0, 1.0), Dict{Symbol, Any}())
    return cell
end
crack_k33(a, a₃) = canonical_components(homogenize(crack_cell(a, a₃, Dict(:K => TensISO{3}(1.0))), MultipoleExpansion(; nmax = 8), :K))[3, 3]
function crack_moduli(a, a₃)
    ν₀ = 0.25
    C₀ = TensISO{3}(2 * (1 + ν₀) / (1 - 2ν₀), 2.0)        # μ₀ = 1
    M = TensND.mandel(homogenize(crack_cell(a, a₃, Dict(:C => C₀)), MultipoleExpansion(; nmax = 4), :C), TensND.CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
    D = inv(M)
    return 1 / (2 * (1 + ν₀) * D[3, 3]), 1 / (2 * D[5, 5])   # D₁₃₁₃ = D[5, 5]/2 in Kelvin–Mandel
end
function crack_tables()
    io = IOBuffer()
    lit = book["tables"]
    println(io, "| ``a`` | ``a_3/a`` | ``\\lambda^*_{33}/\\lambda_0`` |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for row in lit["conductivity_cracks_so"], (r, key) in ((1.0, "1"), (0.5, "1_2"), (0.25, "1_4"))
        row["a1"] in (5.0, 3.0, 2.5) || continue
        println(io, "| ", row["a1"], " | ", r, " | ", @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", crack_k33(row["a1"], r * row["a1"]), row["a3_over_a1_" * key]), " |")
    end
    println(io)
    println(io, "| ``a`` | ``a/a_3`` | ``E^*_{33}/E_0`` | ``\\mu^*_{13}/\\mu_0`` |")
    println(io, "| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
    for a in (5.0, 3.0), (ā, key) in ((1.0, "1"), (2.0, "2"))
        E, μ = crack_moduli(a, a / ā)
        E_ref = only(r["a_over_a3_" * key] for r in lit["young_cracks_so"] if r["a"] == a)
        μ_ref = only(r["a_over_a3_" * key] for r in lit["shear_cracks_so"] if r["a"] == a)
        println(io, "| ", a, " | ", ā, " | ", @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", E, E_ref), " | ", @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", μ, μ_ref), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end
